subtitle: Learn to tell the difference between a consistent rule and an opportunity people can actually use, and to examine practical changes without assuming what another person needs.
scope: For staff throughout DHS. This foundation course explains concepts through practice service and workplace examples. It does not decide eligibility, authorize exceptions, classify protected information or replace required equity analysis, accessibility review or other applicable procedures. Learning here does not automatically count toward required DHS training credit.
introTranscript: Equality and equity both matter in public service. Equality can help us examine whether a standard or opportunity is applied consistently. Equity asks how the design and use of that standard affect access, opportunity and outcomes when people face different barriers. The distinction is useful when reviewing a form, inviting participation or handing off a work task. You will follow a service team that offers one application route, examine who can use it, compare feasible responses and plan an honest evidence review. No person’s identity alone tells you what assistance they need, and a learning exercise does not authorize changing an agency requirement.

lessons.title: Describe equality and equity without making them opposites
lessons.summary: Explain why consistent treatment and attention to barriers can work together.
lessons.objective: Distinguish the course working meaning of equality from the DHS policy meaning of equity.
objectives: Distinguish the course working meaning of equality from the DHS policy meaning of equity.
Explain how an identical process can offer unequal practical access.
Identify an assumption about a person that the distinction does not support.
takeaways: Consistent standards and equitable access can support the same purpose.
A common method does not establish that everyone can use it.
Identity alone does not identify a person’s needs or preferences.
lessons.statement: Ask both whether the rule is consistent and whether the opportunity is usable.

image.caption: Four colleagues stack their hands together over a work table.

intro.heading: Two questions about the same work
intro.body:
In this course, equality is a working description for examining the same status, standard or opportunity: whether a rule applies consistently, for example. Equity adds attention to the barriers, power and practical circumstances that shape access, opportunity and outcomes. DHS’s Equity Policy describes equity as ongoing action rather than a one-time declaration. These ideas are connected; a process can require consistent standards and different ways to participate.

Consider a service team that offers every person the same online form. Staff see an equal invitation because the link and stated deadline are the same. But the invitation alone cannot show whether people can read the instructions, use the form with their assistive technology or obtain the information needed to respond. Examining those conditions does not mean that every person needs a different form or that every rule should be waived. It asks what the process actually requires and where an avoidable barrier may occur.

A person’s disability, language, location or other identity does not tell staff everything about that person’s access, preferences or circumstances. Ask appropriate questions and examine the work rather than assign assistance automatically. People may share a barrier, experience different barriers or prefer different responses.

Use the distinction to make a decision question clearer: What must remain consistent, what prevents usable access and what authorized response could address it? Neither word settles the decision by itself. A proposal needs evidence, affected perspectives and the appropriate authority. The following lessons examine those pieces through the practice form instead of asking learners to label people or certify that a process is fair.

inThisLesson: Separate barriers from assumptions about people.
lessons.keyStatement: A shared purpose can need both consistent standards and usable access.

flashcards.back: A course working description for examining the same status, standard or opportunity; it does not mean every method must be identical.
Ongoing attention and action concerning barriers, power, access, opportunity and outcomes.
Everyone is offered the same route; that alone does not establish usable access.
An untested conclusion about what someone needs, wants or can do.

items.title: Consistency
items.body: Consistent instructions can reduce confusion and arbitrary decisions. In the practice form, staff should explain the applicable requirements accurately to everyone. This useful consistency does not tell them whether the online route itself is usable.

items.title: Usability
items.body: A person may be willing and eligible to participate but unable to operate a form. Examine that route before treating a missed response as lack of interest. The concern is about a work design that can be checked, rather than a label for the person.

items.title: Agency
items.body: People should have an appropriate opportunity to describe a need or preference. Do not choose an alternative solely because someone belongs to a group. A helpful response addresses an identified barrier and preserves the person’s choices within applicable requirements.

tabs.label: Same link
tabs.body: A shared link establishes that the team distributed one route. It does not establish that the route worked for everyone or that required access arrangements were met. Keep distribution evidence separate from usability evidence.

tabs.label: Different route
tabs.body: An alternative route may remove a practical barrier while retaining the same valid requirements. Whether it is available needs the appropriate review; staff cannot simply declare every alternative permissible.

tabs.label: Group label
tabs.body: A label such as older adult or person with a disability is not a complete access assessment. Ask about the task and relevant barrier. A group-level pattern may prompt inquiry without explaining every individual’s experience.

check.question: What can the common link establish?
check.correct: The team offered one route; usable access and applicable requirements still need examination.
wrong: Everyone had the same practical opportunity.
Anyone who did not respond lacked motivation.
Equity requires a different rule for every person.
check.feedbackCorrect: This separates the offered method from its actual usability. Equality and equity questions can both help examine the same process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A common route cannot establish everyone’s access or motive. Equity also does not automatically authorize individualized rules. Identify the requirement, the possible barrier and the next evidence or responsible review.

items.text: State the applicable information requirement clearly.
Use an accurate definition when reviewing each response.
Can the form be used with the person’s assistive technology?
What prevents someone from obtaining the required information?
Every person in this group needs the same assistance.
An identical link proves equitable access.

lessons.next: Next, examine how a common rule can create a practical barrier.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A team calls an online-only invitation equitable because everyone received the same link. No usability evidence has been reviewed.
options: Assume the common link settles both questions.
Identify which requirements must remain consistent and investigate whether the route is usable.
Assign a separate route to everyone based on age.
responses: Distribution is relevant but does not establish usability.
This joins consistency with an evidence-based access question while avoiding automatic exceptions.
Age alone does not establish a need or preference.

lessons.transfer: Describe one practice common process, its legitimate purpose and an access question that remains unanswered.

move.control: You can make the distinction concrete in a work question.
move.failure: The words equality and equity become competing slogans rather than useful ways to examine the work.
move.next: Describe one practice common process, its purpose and an access question.

lessons.title: Examine the requirement and the route separately
lessons.summary: Locate a barrier in a practice process without assuming the underlying requirement is optional.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a service requirement from the method used to collect information.
objectives: Distinguish a service requirement from the method used to collect information.
Trace a task step that could create an avoidable barrier.
Identify an issue needing authorized review before a change.
takeaways: The purpose of a requirement and its delivery method are different questions.
Trace the task rather than explain the difficulty through identity.
A proposed improvement must fit authority and applicable requirements.
lessons.statement: Check whether the route is necessary for the purpose, rather than treating familiarity as proof.

intro.heading: Follow the person through the task
intro.body:
A process contains several choices. A program may require specific information to make an authorized determination, while the team also chooses how to request, receive and review that information. Those choices should not be treated as one inseparable rule. Staff can investigate a barrier in the collection method without promising that the underlying eligibility requirement will disappear.

In the practice service form, the team needs an address and supporting information. The current route requires a person to upload a scan before moving to the next page. A staff member hears that some people have the information but cannot operate that upload step. That is a specific work question: is the upload method necessary, can its accessibility be repaired, and is another authorized way to provide the information available? It is not evidence that the people lack the required information or should receive an automatic favorable decision.

Trace the sequence from invitation to completed response. Identify the instructions, equipment, file format, timing, handoff and review steps. A barrier might occur at one step while the rest of the process works. The location of the difficulty helps the team identify a proportionate response. It also helps avoid an unnecessary replacement of the whole process.

Keep actual legal and program decisions with the appropriate authority. Public-service disability requirements recognize that an identical method may not provide equal opportunity, but the conditions and limits matter. Staff should identify the issue and use the relevant access or program review instead of making a personal exception or declaring that no adjustment can ever be allowed. A clear account of the task is the starting point for that review.

lessons.keyStatement: A difficulty with the method does not establish a failure to meet the requirement.

flashcards.back: The information, condition or decision criterion that applies under the authorized process.
The method used to provide information or participate.
One action or handoff in a larger process.
Confirming who can decide a change and which requirements constrain it.

items.title: Purpose
items.body: Ask why the information is required and which source establishes the requirement. Familiar practice may differ from a binding condition. The course cannot resolve that question for an actual program, but staff can make it explicit for the person responsible.

items.title: Step
items.body: Describe what the person must do at the upload stage. If a scan can be obtained but the form cannot accept it accessibly, that distinction matters. It points to a route issue rather than a conclusion about eligibility or effort.

items.title: Handoff
items.body: An alternative that receives information but loses it before review is not a complete repair. Trace who receives it, how it reaches the authorized decision and what confirmation the person receives. A useful route must work through the handoff.

tabs.heading: Three responses to the upload concern

tabs.label: Keep it without review
tabs.body: Keeping the route because it is familiar avoids a change but leaves the identified issue unanswered. Before defending it as necessary, check its purpose, evidence and applicable access responsibilities.

tabs.label: Waive everything
tabs.body: Waiving the information requirement may appear helpful but can exceed staff authority and alter the decision without a valid basis. Separate the barrier from the requirement and seek an authorized response.

tabs.label: Review the method
tabs.body: A method review examines whether the upload can be repaired or another permitted route can collect the same needed information. Check the full handoff and the person’s access, rather than promise a result before review.

check.question: What does the upload concern show?
check.correct: A particular collection step may create a barrier; the requirement and possible routes need authorized review.
wrong: Everyone with an upload difficulty is ineligible.
All supporting information should be waived.
The familiar route cannot be questioned.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account identifies a specific issue without making an eligibility finding or an unauthorized exception.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An upload difficulty does not settle eligibility or establish that a requirement can be ignored. Familiarity also does not establish necessity. Explain the step and use the relevant review to identify a lawful, usable route.

items.text: Which source establishes the needed supporting information?
Which criterion does the person responsible use?
Can the person operate the upload control?
How does another permitted format reach the person responsible?
Who can authorize an alternative collection route?
Which access responsibilities apply to this service?

lessons.next: Next, consider affected perspectives without assuming a shared need.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: A person has the requested information but cannot use the upload step. A colleague proposes either denying the request immediately or waiving every requirement.
scenario.prompt: What is a sound next step?
options: Describe the step, examine permitted access arrangements and retain the authorized decision criteria.
Infer the person’s capacity from a group label.
responses: Neither shortcut examines the particular barrier and authority.
This connects an access concern to the real process without promising a decision outcome.
A label cannot establish the person’s task experience.

lessons.transfer: Map a practice task as requirement, method, barrier, handoff and responsible review.

move.control: You can identify a specific process question and take it to the appropriate review.
move.failure: An access concern becomes either an automatic denial or an unauthorized waiver.
move.next: Map the requirement and route separately before proposing a change.

lessons.title: Ask about access without assigning needs to a group
lessons.summary: Use affected perspectives to test an access question while preserving choice and privacy.
lessons.objective: Prepare a focused question about a task barrier.
objectives: Prepare a focused question about a task barrier.
Distinguish an individual account from a claim about an entire group.
Plan participation that avoids unnecessary personal disclosure.
takeaways: Ask what happened in the task and what would make participation usable.
One account can reveal a concern without representing every person.
Collect and share only information appropriate to the role and purpose.
lessons.statement: People can describe their own experience without becoming representatives of a group.

image.caption: Four colleagues stack their hands together over a work table.

intro.heading: Hear the experience and test the process
intro.body:
People who use a process can identify a step that a staff-only review misses. Their contribution is evidence to consider, not an invitation to assume that every person sharing an identity has the same experience. Ask about the particular task, the effect of the barrier and a possible response. Avoid making personal disclosure the price of having a concern taken seriously.

In the practice form review, one person describes difficulty navigating the upload control and another describes unclear instructions about an acceptable document. Both accounts matter, but they identify different issues. Fixing the control would not necessarily clarify the instruction, and explaining the instruction would not necessarily make the control usable. The team should record the distinct questions and seek further appropriate evidence.

A focused question might ask which step prevented submission or what happened after the person requested help. It need not ask for a full medical history, income history or every previous service experience. In actual work, staff follow the information collection, privacy and participation procedures that apply to their role. This exercise uses practice accounts so learners do not disclose real service or employee records.

Explain what the team can influence and what it cannot promise. Input may support an existing choice, suggest a change or reveal a question needing another authorized office. Listening does not require agreement with every proposal; it requires an accurate account and a reasoned response. A person can also prefer not to participate in an optional learning or engagement conversation. That preference does not permit ignoring an access duty or withholding a service that the person is otherwise entitled to use.

inThisLesson: Record how input informed the next step.
lessons.keyStatement: A focused account is useful without a universal group claim.

flashcards.back: Knowledge from a person whose participation or work may be affected by the decision.
A question directed to the specific task and next responsibility.
People sharing a category may experience different barriers or preferences.
The part of the decision the team can actually change or refer for review.

items.title: Task question
items.body: Ask which step failed and what happened next. This produces a usable process description without requiring the person to explain a diagnosis or prove group membership. If more information is actually required, follow the appropriate authorized procedure.

items.title: Difference between accounts
items.body: Keep the navigation issue and the unclear-document issue distinct. Combining them into a single story about a group can hide the actual repair needed. Look for shared and different conditions in the work, not a fixed cultural or disability trait.

items.title: Response
items.body: Explain what was learned, what will be checked and what remains open. If input supports an unchanged choice, record the reason. Do not imply that participation guarantees the person’s preferred outcome or that an unanswered concern means the person was unwilling to collaborate.

tabs.label: One volunteer
tabs.body: A volunteer may identify an important barrier. The account does not establish how common the barrier is or represent everyone affected. Use it to form a question and seek appropriate further evidence.

tabs.label: Automatic group assignment
tabs.body: Assigning a person to speak for a group can create pressure and obscure individual preferences. Invite the relevant task experience without demanding an identity explanation or a universal group view.

tabs.label: Several usable routes
tabs.body: Appropriate written, verbal or supported participation methods may bring in different knowledge. Check that each route reaches the decision and meets applicable responsibilities; offering options alone does not establish meaningful participation.

check.question: What should the team record from the two practice accounts?
check.correct: Two distinct barriers, appropriate evidence questions and responsible next steps, without claiming either account represents a whole group.
wrong: One universal need for every person with a disability.
A participation score based on how much personal history each person shared.
Proof that the whole process is unusable for everyone.
check.feedbackCorrect: The record respects each contribution and gives the team specific issues to examine.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Personal disclosure and group labels cannot substitute for task evidence. Two accounts may identify different barriers without proving frequency or everyone’s experience. Record what each account supports and what needs further review.

items.text: The upload control did not accept keyboard navigation in the practice test.
The instruction did not explain the practice document option.
Assign an authorized access check for the control.
Explain why a proposed instruction remains unchanged.
Every person in this category has the same barrier.
More personal disclosure makes a contribution more valid.

lessons.next: Next, compare responses rather than treating any difference as a sound improvement.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: One participant identifies a navigation barrier. The team asks the participant to explain what everyone with the same disability needs.
options: Ask about the specific task and possible response without requiring a group representation.
Require a detailed diagnosis before receiving the concern.
Treat the first account as a complete population survey.
responses: This respects the contribution and supports a testable process question.
Unnecessary medical disclosure is not a prerequisite for examining the task.
One account cannot establish frequency or universal preference.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a task-focused question, an information limit and a sentence describing what one account can and cannot establish.

move.control: You can gather relevant perspectives with accurate limits.
move.failure: An engagement invitation becomes forced disclosure or a stereotype.
move.next: Use a focused practice account to identify a next evidence question.

lessons.title: Compare changes against a shared purpose
lessons.summary: Compare feasible options by their access, burden and authority conditions.
lessons.objective: State the purpose and decision criteria for a practice process.
objectives: State the purpose and decision criteria for a practice process.
Compare benefits and burdens of three response options.
Identify a condition to verify before recommending a change.
takeaways: A different method is not automatically an equitable one.
Check who carries a new burden and how the route reaches a decision.
A recommendation needs a reason and an authority check.
lessons.statement: Choose a response for the barrier it addresses, not for how different it looks.

image.caption: Four colleagues stack their hands together over a work table.

intro.heading: Options need evidence and conditions
intro.body:
After identifying a barrier, compare possible responses against the work’s purpose. A different route is not automatically better, and an identical route is not automatically sufficient. Relevant criteria include usable access, accurate information, privacy, reasonable workload and the authorized decision process. Make those criteria visible before choosing a preferred option.

In the practice form review, staff compare leaving the upload unchanged, repairing the upload control, and adding a permitted assisted-submission route. Leaving it unchanged may preserve a familiar workflow but does not answer the navigation concern. Repairing the control may improve independent use, yet the team must verify the repair and consider other unresolved barriers. An assisted route may help some people but can create a new handoff or dependence if it is poorly designed.

Ask who does extra work, when help is available, how information is protected and whether the person retains an appropriate choice. Do not make a person accept a separate route merely because staff prefer it. Public-service disability rules include limits and responsibilities concerning effective opportunity, integration and choice. Actual arrangements require the relevant review rather than a blanket course promise.

The team may need more evidence before recommending one option. It can describe a conditional recommendation: repair and test the control, check whether an additional permitted route is needed, and identify the responsible person and review point. A condition is useful when it states what must be established. It should not hide an unresolved obligation or become an excuse for an inaccessible release. The goal is a supported, authorized response that addresses the identified barrier while preserving the legitimate purpose of the process.

lessons.keyStatement: A sound recommendation explains benefit, burden, uncertainty and authority.

flashcards.back: A relevant standard used to compare options.
The time, effort, cost or access difficulty an option may place on someone.
A proposal that states what must be verified or authorized before it can proceed.
The person’s appropriate opportunity to participate without an automatic group assignment.

items.title: Barrier fit
items.body: A control repair addresses navigation; it does not necessarily answer unclear instructions or missing information. Identify the specific problem each option addresses and the problem it leaves open. This prevents a visible improvement from being mistaken for a complete solution.

items.title: New burden
items.body: An assisted route may require appointments, travel or repeated disclosure. Trace those steps before describing it as easier. Consider the staff handoff too: information received at one point must reach the authorized person accurately and appropriately.

items.title: Verification
items.body: A repair must be tested through the relevant process. Successful use in one practice example is not a universal guarantee. A clear verification question identifies the task, evidence and responsible review rather than asking for a general impression that the process feels fair.

tabs.label: Leave unchanged
tabs.body: This avoids new implementation work but leaves the known navigation question unresolved. If evidence later shows the method is usable, explain that evidence; do not substitute familiarity or distribution counts for it.

tabs.label: Repair and test
tabs.body: This can support independent use of the common route while retaining the valid requirements. Test the actual problem and review remaining access needs. A technical correction is useful evidence, not automatic completion of every obligation.

tabs.label: Additional permitted route
tabs.body: A second route may remove a particular barrier, but it needs authority, privacy and handoff checks. Do not make the person prove loyalty by using the original route or require a separate route solely based on identity.

check.question: What makes the conditional recommendation useful?
check.correct: It links the proposed response to the barrier, identifies burdens and specifies evidence and authority still needed.
wrong: It produces an unexplained numerical fairness score.
It sends every person in one group to a separate process.
check.feedbackCorrect: The recommendation gives the person responsible something specific to assess and does not pretend uncertainty is resolved.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Novelty, a precise-looking score and group assignment do not establish a sound response. Compare the purpose, barrier, burden, choice and authority, and explain what evidence would support the next decision.

items.text: The repaired control may support independent submission.
A permitted additional route may address a remaining task barrier.
The information handoff reaches the authorized person.
The repair is tested through the relevant access process.
A different route is always equitable.
A common route is always sufficient.

lessons.next: Next, interpret outcome figures without confusing a difference with an explanation.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The team proposes an assisted route but has not checked appointment availability, privacy, handoffs or the person’s choice.
scenario.prompt: What should happen before treating it as a sound response?
options: Declare success because another route exists.
Check its barrier fit, authority, new burdens and full handoff while reviewing the common route.
Require everyone with a disability to use assistance.
responses: Offering a route does not show that it works in practice.
This examines the proposed response instead of relying on its label.
Group assignment can create another barrier and bypass individual choice.

lessons.transfer: Compare three practice options using purpose, barrier, burden, choice, uncertainty and responsible review.

move.control: You can explain why an option deserves consideration and what remains unverified.
move.failure: The appearance of a special response replaces evidence of usable access.
move.next: Write a conditional recommendation with a clear evidence question.

lessons.title: Use evidence without making a difference explain itself
lessons.summary: Interpret a practice rate difference as a question for investigation, not a finding of cause.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a count from a comparable rate.
objectives: Distinguish a count from a comparable rate.
State a possible explanation that remains unverified.
Identify privacy and comparability checks before using actual group data.
takeaways: Counts and rates answer different questions.
A difference can prompt inquiry without establishing its cause.
Use authorized, suitable evidence and protect small groups.
lessons.statement: Describe what the figures show, then name what they cannot explain.

image.caption: Four colleagues stack their hands together over a work table.

intro.heading: A result needs context
intro.body:
A form improvement should be reviewed for its actual use and effect. Counting how many invitations were sent establishes activity, while examining whether people could complete the task addresses a different question. A result should match the question and be interpreted with its limitations.

The practice team records thirty completed responses from forty invitations in one test group and thirty from sixty in another. The same number of completions does not mean the same completion rate: the practice rates are seventy-five percent and fifty percent. The difference is twenty-five percentage points. These numbers illustrate arithmetic, not an official DHS finding or a validated equity score. They do not establish which barrier caused the difference, whether the groups are comparable or whether the process is the only relevant factor.

Possible explanations might involve the invitation list, instructions, available time, information needs or the access route. Treat each as a question requiring evidence. Do not infer that an identity caused a response or that a person who did not complete the task lacked motivation. Also examine who was never invited and whether the measured task represents the intended result.

In actual work, use only evidence authorized for the purpose and role. Check definitions, denominators, periods, missing values, overlapping groups, privacy and small-group protections with the responsible data process. Removing names alone does not make a record safe to share. If a comparison cannot be supported, describe the information gap and next review rather than report reassurance or a causal conclusion. A review can be useful while uncertainty remains, provided the result and its limits are communicated honestly.

lessons.keyStatement: A difference identifies an inquiry; evidence and context determine its interpretation.

flashcards.back: The number of recorded events or people in a defined category.
A count relative to its relevant denominator.
The subtraction of two percentages, distinct from a relative percent change.
Information needed for the question that is absent, unsuitable or unavailable for authorized use.

accordion.heading: Check the result before explaining it

items.title: Denominator
items.body: Thirty completions from forty invitations and thirty from sixty do not represent the same fraction. Confirm what the denominator means. An invitation denominator also excludes people never invited, so it cannot establish population-wide access.

items.title: Comparable groups
items.body: Definitions, time periods and task conditions affect whether a comparison is meaningful. A group receiving a different deadline may not be comparable without context. Keep overlap and missing information visible rather than pool records automatically.

items.title: Cause
items.body: A rate difference does not identify why it occurred. Review the route and affected perspectives alongside appropriate evidence. An observed change after a repair may be relevant, but other changes can also affect the result; do not label the repair the sole cause without support.

tabs.label: Same count
tabs.body: Reporting thirty completions in each group is accurate if clearly defined, but it misses the different invitation totals. State the relevant denominators and the question the measure actually addresses.

tabs.label: Difference with limits
tabs.body: A twenty-five-percentage-point difference accurately describes the practice rates. Add that cause, comparability and people not invited remain unresolved. This supports inquiry without pretending the arithmetic establishes a complete equity analysis.

tabs.label: Cause claim
tabs.body: Saying the difference proves an identity group lacks interest exceeds the figures and introduces a stereotype. The task, invitation and evidence need investigation. Use a supported description and a specific next question instead.

check.question: What can the sample figures establish?
check.correct: The recorded completion rates differ by twenty-five percentage points; the cause and wider access conclusions remain unverified.
wrong: An identity group caused the difference.
The equal completion counts prove equal practical access.
Missing information can be counted as successful participation.
check.feedbackCorrect: The arithmetic is clear and bounded. The difference prompts examination but cannot explain itself.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Counts alone conceal the denominators, and missing information cannot be invented. A group label is not a causal explanation. Describe the rates, the comparison limits and the next evidence needed.

items.text: Thirty of forty practice invitations led to completion.
The practice rates differ by twenty-five percentage points.
Were the invitation conditions comparable?
Which task barrier may have affected completion?
The difference proves the group was unmotivated.
Removing names makes any table public.

lessons.next: Finally, put the distinction into a preparation note with honest next steps.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Staff report the seventy-five-percent and fifty-percent rates as proof that one group does not care about the service.
options: A supported rate description, comparison limits and an evidence question about the process.
A different identity-based explanation with no new evidence.
A reassuring label because thirty people completed in both groups.
responses: This keeps the observation useful while avoiding an unsupported cause or motive.
Another stereotype would not improve the evidence.
The same count does not establish the same rate or practical access.

lessons.transfer: Write the practice rate comparison, two interpretation limits and one authorized evidence question.

move.control: You can distinguish an observed result from its explanation.
move.failure: Arithmetic becomes a causal claim or a reassurance unsupported by the evidence.
move.next: Describe the figures and their limits before recommending a next review.

lessons.title: Prepare an equity question and a responsible next step
lessons.summary: Create a bounded preparation note for a practice case or suitable draft.
lessons.objective: Apply the equality and equity questions to a practice case or suitable draft.
objectives: Apply the equality and equity questions to a practice case or suitable draft.
Distinguish preparation from the required equity analysis for covered actions.
Identify a responsible next step and review question without claiming completion.
takeaways: A useful note connects purpose, barrier, evidence and authority.
Preparation does not certify policy compliance.
Staff do their work with appropriate guidance and follow-through.
lessons.statement: Use the distinction to improve the next decision, while keeping its actual responsibilities visible.

image.caption: Four colleagues stack their hands together over a work table.

intro.heading: A note that supports the real work
intro.body:
The equality and equity distinction becomes useful when it improves a specific decision question. Write a preparation note that identifies the purpose, the standard that must remain consistent, the possible barrier, the evidence available and an option needing review. Keep uncertainty visible and assign a responsible next step rather than declare that the process has become equitable because the note is complete.

For the practice form, a note might explain that the information requirement remains under the authorized service process, the upload route needs an access check, two participant accounts identify different concerns and the completion figures do not establish cause. The next step could be a responsible access and program review of the route and a clarification of the instruction. Follow-through would examine whether the reviewed changes actually worked for the intended task.

Actual DHS work has policy responsibilities beyond this preparation exercise. The Equity Policy requires formal analysis for actions with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for specified leadership approval. The required DHS Analysis or Scan, or a relevant customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director, remains distinct from this course note. Annual requirements and any training-credit decision also remain separate; finishing these lessons does not establish that they are fulfilled.

The One DSD consultant leads the program and supports staff with guidance, knowledge and feedback. Staff build their own capacity to perform equity work, and optional consultation is not a universal permission gate. Use the responsible office when a policy or access process requires it. Practice with the practice case or a suitable draft within your role. A thoughtful question and honest next step are meaningful learning without demanding a live agency decision or a declaration that every issue is resolved.

inThisLesson: Recognize required analysis and responsible offices.
lessons.keyStatement: A complete learning note is preparation evidence, not proof that all duties or outcomes are complete.

flashcards.back: A bounded account of purpose, barrier, evidence, options and next responsibilities.
The formal work required by applicable policy, distinct from this learning note.
Carrying out a responsible action and examining its actual use and effect.
Guidance and feedback that build staff capability without replacing staff responsibilities or formal authority.

items.title: Evidence and limits
items.body: State what the note relies on and what it cannot establish. The two practice accounts describe distinct task experiences; the rates describe a recorded comparison. Neither supplies a complete causal explanation or a legal finding. A clear limit makes the next inquiry more useful.

items.title: Responsibility
items.body: Identify who can check the route, instruction and program criteria. Do not give the consultant authority that belongs to an equity director, an access process or another responsible office. Support and decision authority can be different roles.

items.title: Review
items.body: Choose a question that matches the action. If the control is repaired, verify the task through the relevant process and check remaining barriers. A completed repair or course is activity evidence, not a guarantee of equal outcomes or the end of required analysis.

tabs.heading: Three ways to finish the exercise

tabs.label: Practice
tabs.body: Use the supplied practice form and write the evidence and next steps. This allows complete learning without exposing real participant records or waiting for an actual work decision.

tabs.label: Suitable draft
tabs.body: A draft within your role can make the reflection relevant if its use and information are appropriate. Keep required agency review separate and avoid placing protected records in the exercise. Actual work completion is not a condition of finishing the course.

tabs.label: Compliance declaration
tabs.body: Declaring full compliance because six questions were answered would exceed the exercise. Identify the actual applicable requirement and responsible next step instead. The preparation note can support the work without certifying its completion.

check.question: What should the finished learning note claim?
check.correct: It documents a bounded preparation exercise and responsible next steps; applicable analysis and other duties remain separate.
wrong: Every DHS equity-policy obligation is fulfilled.
The consultant must approve every staff equity question.
The practice rates prove that the service is equitable.
check.feedbackCorrect: This states the learning result accurately while preserving actual roles, evidence limits and policy responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A learning exercise cannot certify all duties or outcomes, and optional consultant guidance is not a universal approval gate. Explain the issue, evidence, proposed next step and applicable responsible review without turning practice into a compliance finding.

items.text: Describe the information purpose and possible upload barrier.
State the practice rate comparison and its limits.
Use the relevant required-analysis process for a covered actual decision.
Identify who can review the proposed access route.
Six learning answers fulfill every policy duty.
Course completion proves equal service outcomes.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to ask clear questions, examine barriers and connect a supported proposal to its responsible review.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: The team finishes its preparation note and wants to label every access and equity obligation complete without the relevant reviews.
scenario.prompt: How should the result be described?
options: As full compliance because the note is complete.
As preparation with specific evidence, limits and responsible next steps, keeping required processes separate.
As worthless until an actual agency decision occurs.
responses: Completing the note does not establish fulfillment of other duties.
This recognizes useful learning while preserving actual work responsibilities.
Practice can produce meaningful understanding without a live decision.

lessons.transfer: Write a preparation note with purpose, consistent requirement, possible barrier, evidence, option, responsible next step and review question.

move.control: You can prepare a clear question and follow the responsibilities that apply to your role.
move.failure: A finished learning activity is mistaken for a complete analysis or an achieved outcome.
move.next: Use the practice case or a suitable draft to record a supported next question and responsibility.

jobAid.subtitle: Examine the common standard, usable opportunity and evidence before proposing a change.
remember: Equality and equity can address different questions about the same work.
An identity label does not establish a need, preference or explanation.
A preparation exercise is distinct from required analysis and authorized decision-making.

sections.heading: Describe the issue
items: Name the legitimate purpose and applicable requirement.
Trace the route and identify the particular task barrier.
Hear affected perspectives without requiring personal disclosure or group representation.

sections.heading: Compare possible responses
items: Check the barrier each option addresses and the burden it may create.
Confirm authority, choice, privacy and the full handoff.
Identify evidence and conditions still needed before a recommendation.

sections.heading: Review honestly
items: State counts, denominators and comparison limits where appropriate.
Treat differences as inquiries rather than automatic cause or motive.
Record how input informed a changed or unchanged choice and the reason.

sections.heading: Follow through
items: Use the actual applicable analysis or access process.
Seek guidance while retaining responsibility for your own work.
Assign a next step and examine its use and effect without certifying universal success.

sources.title: DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Primary definitions of equity, access, inequities and the equity lens, and the distinction between preparation and the formal analysis required for covered actions.

sources.title: 28 CFR 35.130 — General prohibitions against discrimination
sources.note: Current public-service disability provisions show why equal opportunity does not always mean an identical method. Actual decisions follow applicable requirements and authorized review; this course does not decide a legal case.
